newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Congress to watch China's handling of HK - Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Congress to watch China's handling of HK - Gingrich.

text.p: The U.S. Congress will be deeply concerned if China breaches agreements governing Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule on July 1, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Thursday.

"As July 1 approaches, the leaders of Congress would look with deep concern on any action that would undermine the Sino-British Joint Declaration," Gingrich told the American Chamber of Commerce on the fourth day of a 10-day Asian tour.
Britain and China signed the Joint Declaration in 1984. China pledges to grant Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and to retain its capitalist system for 50 years after the handover.
Both Hong Kong and China faced danger and opportunity as the July 1 transition from British to Chinese rule approached, Gingrich said.

A smooth transition would enhance both economic growth and China's international standing, but any failure to honour the handover agreements would endanger China's relationship with Taiwan, the region and the rest of the world, he said.

"And I want to suggest to you that beginning on July 1, Hong Kong has a duty that is historic, because its great economic endeavour can have a moral purpose -- the expansion of freedom," Gingrich said.
China needed to understand that political freedom must accompany economic freedom, and America would not remain silent about the lack of basic freedoms in China, Gingrich said.

"Were we to do so, we would not only betray our own tradition, we would also fail to fulfill our obligations as a friend of both China and Hong Kong. For no one can be considered a true friend if that person avoids the truth," he said.

China's decision to repeal some Hong Kong civil liberties laws threatened to undermine international confidence in the rule of law, one of the foundations of the territory's economic success, Gingrich said.
Any changes -- no matter how small -- to these laws threatened the territory's future prosperity, he added.

Gingrich stressed the importance of maintaining an "open, candid" dialogue with Beijing, his next stop. Any failure by the United States and China to work together would have serious consequences for the next century, he added.
His trip to China follows on the heels of a visit by Vice President Al Gore aimed at healing the damage to U.S.-China ties inflicted by a host of disputes, particularly over Taiwan and human rights.
During his visit, Gore said the United States expected China to live up to its commitments on Hong Kong after the transfer of power.
